title: SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning

Title:SparseGDN: Chunk Sparse in Linear Attention
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) offer linear-time sequence modeling, yet long-context prefill remains costly due to dense intra-chunk computation, recurrent-state updates, and intermediate state storage. We introduce SparseGDN, a hardware-aware framework that combines structured intra-chunk approximation with input-dependent recurrent-event selection while producing outputs for every token. A block-adjacent solver reduces local Delta-solve computation, while a dynamic selector allocates recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The GPU implementation materializes updates only for selected events and reconstructs token outputs using compact state snapshots and group-local interactions, reducing computation and memory traffic. We evaluate SparseGDN on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B across RULER tasks and context lengths from 4K to 128K. Retaining approximately 29% of recurrent events on average, SparseGDN achieves 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels, including online selection overhead.

report.summary: SparseGDN selectively skips most recurrent updates in Gated Delta Networks, speeding long-context prefill by up to 1.94x while preserving per-token outputs.
report.background: Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) are linear-time sequence models that update a recurrent state in chunks rather than using quadratic attention. They are attractive for long-context LLMs, but prefill remains costly because dense intra-chunk delta solves, recurrent-state writes, and intermediate state storage dominate compute and memory traffic at 128K tokens. SparseGDN arrives as inference stacks such as vLLM and SGLang, plus kernel libraries like FLA, compete on time-to-first-token and GPU memory for long-context models. The paper evaluates Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B on RULER, a standard long-context benchmark, indicating a production-style prefill focus rather than toy sequence tasks. It also reflects a broader trend: sparsity and hardware-aware kernels are moving from attention into linear-attention hybrids.
key_points: SparseGDN keeps outputs for every token but only materializes a subset of recurrent-state updates. An input-dependent selector chooses which recurrent events matter, retaining about 29% on average. This turns dense recurrent updates into sparse events, cutting compute and memory traffic without dropping tokens from the output sequence.

The method combines a block-adjacent solver that reduces local Delta-solve work inside chunks with a dynamic budget allocator that distributes recurrent-update budgets across head pairs. The design is hardware-aware, co-designed with GPU memory access and kernel behavior rather than being a purely algorithmic sparsity trick.

On Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, evaluated on RULER at 4K-128K, SparseGDN reports 1.50-1.94x GDN-core prefill speedups over native FLA kernels. The speedups include online event-selection overhead, which matters because selector cost often erodes sparsity gains in practice.

The GPU implementation stores compact state snapshots and reconstructs token outputs through group-local interactions instead of keeping all intermediate recurrent states. This directly targets the memory-bandwidth bottleneck of long-context prefill, where writing and reading state can cost as much as arithmetic.

SparseGDN is evaluated on GDN-core prefill, not full end-to-end serving. It does not claim wall-clock gains for decoding or complete inference, so production impact depends on integration with serving frameworks and whether the sparsity holds across tasks beyond RULER.
report.impact: If reproduced, SparseGDN could shift long-context competition from model size toward kernel efficiency. For the AI industry, it validates that linear-attention models can be sparsified at the recurrent-state level, not just in attention maps. For developers, the value is a blueprint—dynamic event selection, compact snapshots, and group-local reconstruction—that can be ported to other GDN and state-space kernels. For regular users, the near-term effect is lower latency and cost for long-document chat, codebase analysis, and RAG prefill, not new capabilities. Caveats matter: results are on RULER and GDN-core prefill; full serving, decoding, and quality at 29% retention need independent verification.
report.tools: Watch the flash-linear-attention (FLA) repository for GDN kernels, Qwen3.5 model cards, and the RULER benchmark harness. Triton is the likely path for reproducing the GPU kernels; vLLM and SGLang are the serving stacks where prefill speedups would matter. No official SparseGDN code is listed in the abstract, so check the paper's arXiv page for updates before building on it.
